extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and correspondents (including country correspondents and feature writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing feature stories and correspondence dispatches for newspapers, including news judgment, formats for mail/telephone/telegraph, deadlines, and handling of copy for printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for feature stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Use varied sources such as stories of the town/state from the past, travelers just returned from foreign countries or distant U.S. sections, educational journals, forestry publications, mining statistics, geological surveys, court decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs add value. The only requirement in obtaining information is personal observation and investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of the feature story (leads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature story form is anomalous; a writer may begin in any way likely to attract and continue to hold the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal leads that arrest attention by telling enough to excite curiosity without giving all details are often used. Examples of suspensive leads are provided (short dramatic headlines followed by atmospheric copy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense-story technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Some feature stories aim to hold readers' interest by making the narrative suspensive throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a suspensive tone across the narrative so curiosity is prolonged; examples illustrate how to build and sustain suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of style as a device
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may resort to uniqueness of form or style to achieve effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconventional headings, structure, or terse lines (illustrative example: very short stanza-like lines) can create interest and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain unity of impression through close adherence to a single tone or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape the story consistently (tone, mood, emphasis) so the reader receives one dominant impression (example: a story of pathos or childish loyalty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should write feature stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature stories in supplements are generally written by regular staff, regular contributors, or occasional specialists; news-column features are by stronger reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners should try human-interest types once acquainted with surroundings and dexterity; success in features can lead to advanced pay and prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence work overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondence stories are similar in style and construction to other news stories but are valued differently due to individual transmission and the need for correspondents to work with less supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many reporters, especially in country papers, must learn to gather, write, and file correspondence; it is highly advisable that every newspaper man know correspondence work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating the worth of news (news judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The correspondent must be discriminating in judging news—know the difference between nationally and merely locally interesting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put yourself in the reader's place at the paper's city; assess whether the item would interest someone unfamiliar with local persons/places. Example: a minor local loss is not worth sending unless circumstances make it of wider interest (e.g., involvement in a plot to blow up a bridge).

rubrics_metrics.name: What not to send
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sending merely local items and trivial events: minor accidents, burglaries, robberies; obituaries, marriages, entertainments, court trials of little-known persons; ordinary murders; county fairs, fraternal meetings, high-school commencements; crop/weather unless markedly abnormal; praise-of-individuals/press-agent stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress stories trespassing good taste or decency. Local gossip affecting reputations should be held until verified. Sensational news must be carefully investigated before being put on the wires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rumors (Associated Press guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rumor of sensational news should not be held too long for verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rumor is not libelous, send it immediately as a rumor with an addition that 'the story is being investigated.' If it involves possibly libelous charges against persons or firms, send a note to editors marked 'Private, not for publication' stating the story is being investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to send (tailoring to paper specialties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond big news, correspondents should learn the special types of news particular papers want by studying their columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different papers specialize in different beats (freak news, sporting news, educational news, human interest, local history, animal stories, college sports, liquor sales, etc.). Send items that match the paper's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conducting a local column
rubrics_metrics.description: When running a locality column, never state that there is little news; readers must not suspect scarce information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine local sources for humorous incidents, reminiscences, pioneer stories, war recollections, and community-related feature stories to fill the column, increase subscriptions, and earn money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories by mail: when and how
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the mail for stories whose publication time is not important (feature stories, advance speeches, elections, state celebrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mail arrives by 10:00 A.M. for afternoon papers and 8:00 P.M. for morning papers; use special delivery for big stories; when sending photos use special delivery and wire the paper that pictures are coming; for advance speeches specify exact release day/hour and wire definite release when given; maintain future books and keep state/telegraph editors informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories by telephone: rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the telephone when mail is too slow, telegraph is inconvenient, or personal communication with the office is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call with a jumble of facts. Long-distance calls are costly; have the story written or sketched first so you can dictate concisely and minimize time/cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories by telegraph: use and query format
rubrics_metrics.description: The telegraph is for stories requiring immediacy; certain rules govern their handling, including how to send a 'query' (bulletin) to the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example query format: give concise facts, the intended length (e.g., 'Four hundred.'), and the filing time. Bulletins should state facts plainly (not vague phrases) so the editor can publish immediately if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing while waiting for telegraph reply
rubrics_metrics.description: While waiting for the editor's reply to a query, the correspondent should begin and, if possible, finish the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place most important details first so the story can be shortened from the end if fewer words are ordered; do not omit small words to save telegraph costs—savings are offset by extra editing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey telegraph word limits and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When the paper replies with a requested length (e.g., 'Rush three hundred banker's death.'), you must keep the story within that limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sending more than the ordered length risks reprimand or discharge; prepare to edit rapidly to meet exact orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no reply to query
rubrics_metrics.description: No reply may mean the story is not wanted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible reasons: covered by wire services, the bulletin itself sufficed, or crowded out by more important news. Consider press-time pressures; a late arrival may be refused due to column value increasing near press time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hours and deadlines for filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Know extreme filing hours for various editions to catch them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For afternoon papers: be with telegraph operator by 9:00 A.M. for noon edition, 12:00 M. for 3:00 P.M., 2:00 P.M. for 5:00 P.M. edition; extraordinary news may be filed as late as 2:30. Afternoon papers practically close to correspondents after 12:30–1:00 P.M. Mark late news 'N.P.R.' (night press rate) to send after 6:00 P.M. For morning papers news may be filed as late as 2:00 A.M., though columns close after midnight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling big news by telegraph
rubrics_metrics.description: When big, unquestioned-interest news breaks, bulletin a lead immediately with probable length and filing time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Then follow rapidly with instalments of the detailed story without waiting for reply. Editors prefer too much rather than too little; installments should be sent marked 'More' and final instalment '30'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed telegraphed story format (instalments)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the bulletin lead, send details in instalments, each marked 'More' except the last, which is marked '30'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear timestamps and bylines in each instalment; the telegrapher's '30' signals completion of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sporting news rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute impartiality in controversies; present simple facts only without editorializing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File afternoon scores by 7:30 P.M. (8:00 P.M. outside limit); ensure utmost accuracy in box scores; verify any seeming new records before telegraphing them—if in doubt, report as 'what is said to be a record.' Avoid reporting merely local high-school contests or limited-interest sporting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instructions for correspondents (enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of practical rules to guide correspondent behavior and dispatch handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Forward time stories, manuscripts, cuts by mail (express companies don't deliver at night). 2) In telegrams spell out round numbers; mark beginning of speeches by 'quote' and end by 'end quote.' 3) Keep telegraph companies informed of address/phone; maintain friendly relations with operators. 4) Finish all incomplete stories—clarify false alarms later. 5) Locate scenes accurately using landmarks in addition to street locations. 6) Incurring reasonable expense for big stories is acceptable. 7) Never forget the worth of sending time—every minute is valuable. 8) Until first check, clip and keep every printed story; some papers require sending 'string' for payment; rates vary per column.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of copy and consult the style-book
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy is any manuscript prepared for printing and written according to a newspaper's individual style rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On starting work, ask for the office style-book. If present, study it and write stories according to it; if the paper lacks a style-book, study the columns and changes made to your stories to learn individual office rules. Observe printed rules even if they conflict with general usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typewriter proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of how to handle a typewriter dexterously is a primary requirement in preparing copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are usually furnished typewriters; longhand copy is rarely sent—if longhand is used, it should be very legible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longhand copy legibility and marking unusual words
rubrics_metrics.description: When forced to use longhand, write with painstaking care for accuracy and legibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print unusual proper names and technical words letter by letter. If possible confusion (o vs a, u vs n) may occur, underscore/overscore letters to clarify. Enclose quotation marks in half-circles to show beginning/end. Use a small cross instead of a period or enclose the period in a circle to avoid miscopying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper selection for copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose suitable writing paper when the office does not supply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer unglazed paper of neutral tint (gray, yellow, manila brown), commonly unruled print paper 6x9 or 8½x11 inches, firm enough for ink or pencil. Offices often furnish stationery and self-addressed envelopes for correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins for copy pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave space on copy pages for headline writing, corrections, pasting, and paging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First page: top half left blank for headline. All sheets: 1 inch margin at bottom and each side; sheets other than the first: 1 inch margin at top. Side margins allow for copy-editor corrections; bottom margins for pasting; top margins for paging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph indentation and marking
rubrics_metrics.description: All paragraphs, including the first, should be indented an inch and marked with the paragraph sign (a rectangle) before the first word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two paragraphs are run together, insert the paragraph symbol immediately before the new paragraph's first word and write the symbol in the margin. If a paragraph completes a page, put a paragraph sign at the end to indicate to the compositor a broken line conclusion. Quotations and summaries are exceptions to indentation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and continuity marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When consolidating paragraphs or making separately written matter continuous, indicate the change clearly for the compositor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw a line from the end of the first to the beginning of the second and mark 'No #' in the margin (or similar house method). If a sentence ends at the foot of a sheet but continues on the next page, draw diagonal lines to indicate continuity between pages.
